To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the within-session changes in instrumental responding are determined by the sum of the rates programmed for each component of a multiple schedule and the sum of the reinforcement rates programmed for the two concurrent components of a concurrent schedule.

the number of changeovers and the rates of instrumental responding change within sessions in the same manner during concurrent variable-interval and single variable-interval schedules that provide the same number of reinforcers.

the rate of responding and the number of changeovers change in a similar manner during concurrent variable-interval and simple variable-interval schedules when the sum of the rates programmed by the concurrent variable-interval schedule equals the rate programmed by the simple variable-interval schedule.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model for the control of concurrent variable-interval performance.
the effects of concurrent schedules on behavior, and the effects of behavior on concurrent schedules.
the effects of concurrent schedules of reinforcement on instrumental and changeover behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the concurrent variable-interval schedule of reinforcement is not the same as the sum of the simple variable-interval schedules of reinforcement that are being run concurrently.
concurrent variable-interval (VI) schedules are a special type of multiple schedule.

the within-session changes in the rates of responding and changeovers during concurrent variable-interval schedule are similar to those during variable-interval schedules that provide the same number of reinforcers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
concurrent VI schedules are not simple schedules, and that changeovers are not simple behavior.

concurrent variable-interval (VI) schedules are a good way to study the behavior of animals in the presence of multiple VI schedules, and the results of such studies are consistent with the idea that the within-session behavior of the animal in the presence of each component of a multiple schedule is determined by the sum of the rates programmed by all of the components.

changeovers are controlled by a single process, the same process that controls instrumental responding, and that this process is determined by the sum of the rates at which reinforcers are delivered by all concurrent schedules.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the within-session changes in responding during a component of a concurrent variable-interval schedule are determined primarily by the number of reinforcers obtained in that component, and not by the number of changeovers.
the within-session changes in instrumental behavior are not unique to the concurrent schedules, but rather they are a general phenomenon.
the rate of responding during concurrent schedules is determined by the sum of the rates programmed by each of the concurrent components.
